title: In Order
blurb: Seven Microsoft Sentinel build sequences, from onboarding a workspace to silencing a noisy rule. Each rung only works because the rung under it already happened, so reconstruct the dependency chain rather than the tidy-sounding story.
source: Microsoft Learn Sentinel documentation — workspace onboarding; Content hub solutions; Syslog and CEF via AMA; Windows Security Events via AMA plus data collection rules and Windows Event Forwarding; custom text-file log tables; automation rules and playbooks; data tiers and retention · SC-500 outline 4.2

ladders.title: Standing up a brand-new Sentinel workspace at a regional credit union
ladders.prompt: A four-person security team at a regional credit union has an Azure subscription and nothing else. Put the build in the order that Azure actually permits: each rung creates the resource or the permission that the next rung needs before it can be selected in the portal. The one pure setting change goes at the earliest point where it is both possible and free.
ladders.citation: Learn: Sentinel workspace onboarding quickstart · outline 4.2

steps.label: Confirm the engineer holds Contributor on the subscription that will host the workspace
steps.detail: Enabling the service is a subscription-scoped write, so nothing later in this ladder is even clickable without it. Microsoft Sentinel Contributor on the resource group is the role that governs day-to-day use and content hub installs, and it cannot be granted on a resource group that does not exist yet.

steps.label: Create the Log Analytics workspace in the chosen region and resource group
steps.detail: Sentinel is an add-on to a workspace, never a standalone resource, so the workspace has to exist before the service can be attached. Region matters permanently here because the workspace pins where the data lives, and once Sentinel is on it the workspace cannot be moved to a different resource group or subscription.

steps.label: Add Microsoft Sentinel to that workspace
steps.detail: This is the step that turns a plain monitoring workspace into a SIEM instance, which is what makes the Content hub, Analytics and Automation pages appear at all. Default workspaces created by Defender for Cloud are excluded from the picker, so choosing the purpose-built workspace in the previous rung is what makes this one succeed.

steps.label: Raise retention from the 30-day default toward 90 days
steps.detail: A new workspace still starts at a 30-day default, which quietly clips hunting and rule lookback windows. The first 90 days of retention only come at no extra charge once Sentinel is on the workspace, so the earliest point where the change is both possible and free is straight after the previous rung, before any data starts arriving and ageing out.

steps.label: Decide the portal experience and note whether the workspace was auto-onboarded to the Defender portal
steps.detail: New tenants whose engineer holds subscription Owner or User Access Administrator get their workspace pulled into the Defender portal automatically, and that determines which set of documented navigation paths the rest of the build follows. Settle it before configuring content, because a primary workspace in the Defender portal changes where incidents are created and which connectors must be left disconnected.

steps.label: Install the Azure Activity solution from the Content hub
steps.detail: The connector, its analytics rule templates and its workbooks all ship inside the solution package, so the connector page cannot be opened until the package is installed. Installing here also means the rule templates are already present when the team wants to generate test data on the next rung.

steps.label: Open the Azure Activity connector and run the Azure Policy assignment wizard, scoping the subscription and pointing it at the workspace
steps.detail: The policy assignment is what actually pushes activity records into the workspace, and its Parameters tab needs the workspace resource that rung two created. Only after the assignment deploys does the connector status flip to Connected, which is the signal that later rungs can rely on real data.

steps.label: Enable a rule template from the solution and query the AzureActivity table to prove the pipeline
steps.detail: Verification belongs last because it tests every earlier rung at once: permission, workspace, service, solution and policy assignment. Enabling a shipped detection such as the suspicious resource deployment template also generates the activity that makes the query return rows rather than an empty result.

ladders.title: Getting Common Event Format from a hospital firewall pair into CommonSecurityLog
ladders.prompt: A hospital group needs its perimeter firewalls to reach Sentinel through a dedicated Linux log forwarder. Order the build so that every component exists before something is asked to point at it, and so the appliances are only re-aimed once there is something listening.
ladders.citation: Learn: Syslog and Common Event Format via AMA connectors for Microsoft Sentinel · outline 4.2

steps.label: Build the dedicated Linux forwarder VM and, because it sits on-premises, install the Azure Arc Connected Machine agent
steps.detail: The forwarder must be a manageable Azure resource before it can appear in any resource picker, and a non-Azure machine only becomes selectable through Arc. Skipping Arc is the classic cause of the forwarder simply not being listed later, which blocks the data collection rule outright.

steps.label: From the Content hub, install the solution that carries Common Event Format
steps.detail: The CEF via AMA connector arrives packaged inside that solution, so the connector page it provides does not exist until the install completes. Choosing between the Syslog and the Common Event Format solution here also fixes which table the messages will land in downstream.

steps.label: Confirm the engineer holds the roles that agent deployment and rule authoring each require
steps.detail: Deploying the agent onto machines and Arc-enabled servers, and creating or editing a data collection rule, are separate permission surfaces held by different built-in roles such as Virtual Machine Contributor, Azure Connected Machine Resource Administrator and Monitoring Contributor. Discovering a missing role halfway through the rule wizard means starting the wizard again.

steps.label: Create the data collection rule from the connector page, selecting the forwarder as its resource
steps.detail: The rule is where the destination workspace and the target machines are bound together, and the machine list draws on the Arc registration from the first rung. Creating the rule is also what triggers the Azure Monitor Agent to be pushed onto the forwarder, so the agent install is an outcome of this step rather than a prerequisite for it.

steps.label: Choose the minimum severity per facility on the Collect tab, keeping CEF facilities distinct from plain syslog facilities
steps.detail: Filtering at the rule rather than after ingestion is what keeps the bill and the query surface sane, and the facility split has to be decided now because reusing one facility for both formats duplicates records across CommonSecurityLog and Syslog. If the appliance vendor will not let its facility be changed, the fallback is an ingestion-time transformation added to the rule, which again is easier before data starts flowing.

steps.label: Run the installation script on the forwarder to configure rsyslog or syslog-ng and open the listening port
steps.detail: The daemon only accepts messages from other machines once the script has reconfigured it and opened port 514 for both protocols, and the script assumes the agent it hands logs to is already present. On agent versions from 1.28.11 onward the daemon passes messages to the agent over TCP port 28330 rather than a local socket, so the daemon and agent must be configured as a matched pair.

steps.label: Re-point the firewalls from their own local syslog daemon to the forwarder
steps.detail: This is deliberately the last change on the network side: sending production firewall logs at a host that is not yet listening simply discards them. Once the forwarder is receiving, the appliances can be cut over one at a time with a working target to verify against.

steps.label: Query CommonSecurityLog and reconcile TimeGenerated against EventTime before declaring the connector healthy
steps.detail: Verification comes after the cutover because only real appliance traffic proves the whole chain. The two timestamps can diverge when the forwarder and the appliance sit in different time zones, so noticing that now prevents an analyst from mis-reading an incident timeline months later.

ladders.title: Collecting Windows Security events from a manufacturer's on-premises domain controllers
ladders.prompt: A manufacturer wants domain controller sign-in and process-creation events in Sentinel without paying to ingest every audit record. Order the work so that filtering decisions are made before data volume is committed, not after the first invoice.
ladders.citation: Learn: Windows agent-based data connectors for Sentinel · outline 4.2

steps.label: Onboard the on-premises domain controllers to Azure Arc
steps.detail: Any machine that is not an Azure virtual machine has to be Arc-enabled before an agent-based connector can reach it, and the requirement applies to physical servers and on-premises or third-party-cloud virtual machines alike. Doing it first is what makes the servers appear in the scope picker during the rule wizard.

steps.label: Install the matching solution from the Content hub so the Windows Security Events connector is available
steps.detail: The connector page, with its Configuration area and its Add data collection rule control, only exists once the solution is installed. Every later rung in this ladder is performed from that page.

steps.label: Draft and test the event filter locally with the Get-WinEvent cmdlet and its XPath parameter
steps.detail: Testing on the machine tells the engineer whether the expression is syntactically valid and whether it actually matches events, and it costs nothing. Doing this before the wizard matters because a rule that silently matches nothing looks identical to a healthy rule with a quiet estate, and the platform accepts version 1.0 XPath only, so unsupported functions have to be caught here.

steps.label: Create the data collection rule and name its subscription and resource group
steps.detail: The rule is an independent Azure resource, so it can live in a different subscription or resource group from the servers it governs as long as they share a tenant. Deciding its home now is what lets one rule be reused across environments rather than rebuilt per estate.

steps.label: Add the domain controllers on the Resources tab
steps.detail: This association is the link between the abstract rule and the actual machines, and the agent gets installed on any selected machine that lacks it. The list is populated by the Arc registration from the first rung, so a missing server here almost always means a missing Arc agent rather than a portal fault.

steps.label: On the Collect tab choose Minimal, Common, All events, or Custom with the tested expressions
steps.detail: This choice, not any later query, decides ingestion cost, because the agent filters at the source and leaves the rest on the machine. Minimal drops sign-out records to keep volume down while keeping breach-relevant events, whereas Common preserves a full audit trail, so the answer follows from whether the manufacturer needs auditing or detection.

steps.label: Create the rule and let the agent deploy
steps.detail: Nothing is collected until the rule is validated and created, which is also the moment the agent lands on the newly selected servers. Creation is placed after the filter decision because rewriting a live rule means re-validating expressions against machines that are already sending.

steps.label: Query the SecurityEvent table, then add the Windows Forwarded Events path only if a collector is in play
steps.detail: The Sentinel connector routes these records to SecurityEvent rather than the general Event table, so a successful query here proves the whole chain end to end. Where the estate already forwards to a Windows Event Collection host, that separate connector needs the collector service running with the agent on the collector itself, and the normalization parsers are worth deploying at that point.

ladders.title: Bringing a logistics firm's appliance text log into a custom table
ladders.prompt: A logistics operator runs a security appliance that writes to flat text files and has no ready-made solution. Reconstruct the build order, keeping in mind that one thing must be created by hand before the collection rule can be told where to put the data.
ladders.citation: Learn: Custom Logs via AMA text-file collection · outline 4.2

steps.label: Create the destination table by hand, with a name carrying the custom suffix and exactly two columns
steps.detail: The rule's output stream has to resolve to a real table, so this comes first or the rule has nowhere to write. The table takes a timestamp column and a single string column holding the whole message, and where a forwarder sits in the path that string column is named for the forwarded message rather than the raw payload, which is a choice that cannot be made later without rebuilding.

steps.label: Install the Custom Logs via AMA solution, or the vendor solution if one exists for this appliance
steps.detail: The connector that exposes the file-pattern and transformation fields ships in that solution. Checking for a vendor-specific solution first is worth the minute, because a listed device type auto-fills both the table name and the correct transformation on a later rung.

steps.label: Confirm the roles for agent deployment and rule authoring, and note that this connector is a preview feature
steps.detail: The same role split as other agent-based connectors applies, covering machine-scoped agent deployment and the rule-editing permission. Establishing preview status now shapes whether the firm is willing to put a production detection on top of the table at the end of the ladder.

steps.label: Create the data collection rule and select the machine hosting the application, or the forwarder in front of it
steps.detail: The rule needs a concrete collection point, and a machine that is not an Azure virtual machine has to carry the Connected Machine agent to be listed. The agent is installed as part of the rule deployment, so this rung is what puts collection software on the host.

steps.label: Set the file pattern to the path and filename of the appliance logs, wildcards included
steps.detail: The agent watches paths, not applications, so an incorrect pattern produces a healthy-looking rule with an empty table. This has to be set within the rule because the agent reads its instructions from the rule at runtime.

steps.label: Supply the transformation, or leave the auto-filled one untouched for a recognised device type
steps.detail: The transformation is what shapes each line into the table's schema, so it belongs with the rule that owns the output stream. For a listed device the field is populated correctly on selection and editing it breaks the mapping the table was created to accept.

steps.label: If a forwarder is used, run the daemon configuration script on it and open the listening port
steps.detail: The forwarder only accepts messages from the appliance after its syslog daemon has been reconfigured, and the script assumes the agent from the rule deployment is already in place. Leaving this until after the rule exists avoids configuring a listener that has nowhere to hand its messages.

steps.label: Point the appliance at the collection path and confirm rows appear in the custom table
steps.detail: The appliance is retargeted last so no production log is thrown away against a target that is not ready. Rows landing in the custom table are the proof that the manual table, the file pattern and the transformation all agree with one another.

ladders.title: An insurer wires a Teams-notification playbook to high-severity incidents
ladders.prompt: An insurer wants a single automation rule that triages new high-severity incidents and then calls a playbook to notify the on-call channel. Order the build so that the playbook is selectable when the rule needs it, and so the actions inside the rule run in a sequence that makes sense.
ladders.citation: Learn: Create and use Sentinel automation rules · outline 4.2

steps.label: Create the playbook on the incident trigger in Azure Logic Apps
steps.detail: The trigger type chosen here is binding: only incident-trigger playbooks appear in an incident-trigger automation rule, and only alert-trigger playbooks appear in an alert-trigger rule. Because the rule wizard has to be abandoned and restarted if the playbook does not yet exist, building it first saves the whole configuration.

steps.label: Grant Microsoft Sentinel access to the resource group holding the playbook
steps.detail: Automation rules run playbooks under a dedicated Sentinel service account rather than the analyst's identity, and that account needs explicit rights on the playbook's resource group before any rule can call it. Until that is done the playbook is greyed out in the rule's drop-down, and the engineer who grants it needs Owner on the resource group — the automation role goes to the Sentinel service principal, not to a person — so the approval conversation is worth starting early.

steps.label: Choose the trigger, incident created rather than incident updated
steps.detail: The trigger determines which conditions the wizard will even offer, so it is settled before any condition is written. The update trigger adds state-change operators and an updated-by property that the create trigger has no use for, and rules on the two triggers sit in separate execution queues.

steps.label: Define the conditions on severity and on the analytics rule that generated the incident
steps.detail: Conditions must follow the trigger because the available property and operator sets differ between them. Naming the source detection by analytics rule rather than by incident title is the sturdier condition, since titles drift and the rule name is stable.

steps.label: Add the native triage actions first, changing status and assigning an owner
steps.detail: Actions inside a rule execute strictly in the order they are listed, so the cheap in-product changes are put ahead of the external call. That way the incident is already owned and marked active in the queue even if the notification path is slow.

steps.label: Add the run playbook action after the triage actions
steps.detail: The external call goes last because the engine does not wait indefinitely for it: a playbook running beyond two minutes lets the rule advance regardless of whether it finished. Any action placed after a long-running playbook can therefore execute while that playbook is still in flight.

steps.label: Set the order number for the rule, and an expiration date only if the automation is genuinely temporary
steps.detail: The order value decides where this rule sits among other rules of the same trigger type, and that matters because a rule running earlier can change the very properties this rule's conditions test. Rules created outside the portal do not get an order assigned for them, and identical order numbers within a queue leave the sequence to chance.

steps.label: Verify by querying the SecurityIncident table for changes attributed to automation
steps.detail: Verification is last because it needs a real incident to have passed through the whole chain of trigger, conditions, native actions and playbook. Filtering the incident history on the modifying party separates what the rule did from what an analyst did, which is the only reliable way to audit a silent automation.

ladders.title: A university SOC silences a rule that fires every night during patching
ladders.prompt: A university SOC is drowning in benign incidents from one detection that fires during the nightly maintenance window. Order the tuning work so that the noise is understood before it is suppressed, and so the suppression cannot outlive the maintenance project that caused it.
ladders.citation: Learn: Automate threat response with automation rules · outline 4.2

steps.label: Establish that the recurring incidents are genuinely benign and share a common signature
steps.detail: Suppression closes incidents unread, so the case for it has to be made before anything is automated. Identifying the shared entities and the originating detection is also what supplies the conditions the rule will be built from two rungs later.

steps.label: Open the offending incident and create the automation rule from the incident itself
steps.detail: Starting from the incident rather than the Automation page pre-populates the rule with the incident's name, the analytics rule that produced it and its entities as conditions. That saves reconstructing by hand exactly the signature that was just characterised, and it also proposes a closing action and an expiration date as defaults.

steps.label: Trim the pre-filled conditions down to the ones that describe the maintenance activity
steps.detail: The generated conditions describe one specific incident, which is narrower than the recurring pattern, so they need widening or pruning before the rule generalises. This is done before the actions are set, because an over-broad condition set combined with an automatic close is how a real detection gets buried.

steps.label: Set the close action with an explicit closing reason and a comment naming the maintenance window
steps.detail: The closing reason is what later feeds the team's false-positive analysis, so it belongs in the rule rather than in a wiki. The comment is the only evidence a future analyst will have that the incident was closed by policy and not overlooked.

steps.label: Add a tag that classifies these incidents as patching noise
steps.detail: Tagging sits alongside the close so both happen in one pass over the incident, and it is what makes the suppressed population countable afterwards. Without it, the closed incidents blend into every other closed incident and the tuning cannot be measured.

steps.label: Set an expiration date matching the end of the maintenance project
steps.detail: A time-limited rule disables itself when the window closes, which is what stops a temporary suppression becoming a permanent blind spot. Setting it at authoring time is the only reliable moment, because nobody returns to a rule that is quietly working.

steps.label: Place the rule in the create-trigger queue ahead of rules that act on severity
steps.detail: Later rules see the incident as earlier rules left it, so a suppression that runs first prevents downstream escalation or paging rules from ever evaluating a closed incident. Getting the order wrong here means the on-call phone still rings before the incident is closed.

ladders.title: A retailer right-sizes retention on a very chatty network table
ladders.prompt: A retailer finds one network table dominating its Sentinel bill while analysts rarely query it past a fortnight. Order the retention change so that evidence precedes the decision and so nothing irreversible happens before the reversible parts are proven.
ladders.citation: Learn: Manage Sentinel data tiers and retention · outline 4.2

steps.label: Read Table insights on the Tables page to find which tables actually drive the volume
steps.detail: The observability view surfaces ingestion by tier, the heaviest tables by daily volume and estimated daily cost, which is what turns a suspicion into a target. It is explicitly an investigation surface rather than a billing record, so it identifies the candidate but does not settle the final number.

steps.label: Confirm with the detection owners which analytics rules, hunting queries and workbooks read that table
steps.detail: Real-time features are exactly what a tier change removes, so the dependency list has to exist before the tier is touched. Doing this after the change means discovering the breakage through silent detections rather than through a conversation.

steps.label: Decide the analytics retention window that the live detections genuinely need
steps.detail: Analytics retention is the hot window that alerting, hunting and workbooks all draw on, and it can be extended toward two years at a long-term charge, with Sentinel solution tables reaching ninety days at no cost. This number is chosen first because total retention is measured against it.

steps.label: Work out what total retention the compliance policy actually obliges the retailer to keep on this table
steps.detail: By default the analytics data is mirrored into the lake for the same period, and the lake tail can be set independently and stretched much further at low cost. Pinning the obliged figure after the analytics window is what lets the retailer separate a short hot window from a long cold tail, and it is the number the two remaining changes are measured against.

steps.label: Shorten analytics retention while leaving total retention untouched
steps.detail: This is the milder half of the change and it bites at once: shortening the hot window on a table that already holds data applies immediately, so the older records leave the expensive tier that day, though they survive in the lake out to the total retention boundary and can be promoted back with a job. It comes before any tier switch because the table itself stays in the analytics tier, so the live detections listed two rungs earlier keep running while the saving lands.

steps.label: Move the table to the Data Lake tier only once the dependent content has been reworked
steps.detail: The tier switch is the sharp edge, because real-time analytics and hunting queries against that table stop working the moment it lands. It is last because everything before it can be undone quietly, whereas this one is felt immediately by the analysts on shift.

steps.label: Trim total retention down to what the retention policy actually requires, then leave the change alone for a month
steps.detail: Cutting the lake tail is saved until last because it is the only step that eventually destroys records, so it waits until the hot window and the tier are both settled and the true compliance floor is known. A cut like this is not carried out on the spot: roughly a month passes before the data is actually removed, so a mistyped figure can still be put back, and treating that pause as part of the change is what keeps the whole sequence recoverable.
